newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels are heavily armed - police.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels are heavily armed - police.

text.p: The Marxist guerrillas who seized the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru are heavily armed and a police source said on Friday officials feared they could repel any attempt to storm the building and free the hostages.

The guerrillas have assault rifles and pistols, and three of them are snipers whose weapons are equipped with infrared sights, a senior police officer told Reuters while asking not to be identified. "They have arms enough," he said.
Crack Peruvian troops are preparing for a possible attack on the residence to free the nearly 400 hostages, but will only be used if there is no alternative, the officer said.
President Alberto Fujimori has said that his first priority is "the safeguarding of the health and life of those who are inside," but has not ruled out force.

As the Lima embassy residence is considered Japanese territory, international law would require any military operation against the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) fighters to be approved by the Japanese government.
The police officer said one of the guerrilla snipers was posted at a small second floor window. The light there was not turned on all night.
There are at least 15 guerrillas inside the residence, but there could be more. Police believe any rescue force would need to outnumber the guerrillas by at least 10 to one.
The rebels have spread themselves out over the first and second floors, but the majority are on the second floor, where they are keeping their most important hostages.

Peru's anti-terrorist police think that MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini directed the spectacular attack on the embassy cocktail party on Tuesday night via cellular phone from a base somewhere in Lima.

The police officer said the guerrilla force was made up of fighters from the "Atahualpa Front" in Chanchamayo province, 220 miles (350 km) east of Lima in the Amazon jungle. They apparently arrived in the capital weeks ago, shaking off police intelligence which at first detected their arrival.
The rebels demand that jailed comrades be released near their jungle stronghold, safe from the reach of the army.

Fujimori has refused to give in to the demands and has held war cabinet meetings since Wednesday with top generals, senior intelligence officers and ministers in army headquarters to plan his course of action.

The police officer said authorities have been receiving advice from U.S. experts. In the event that they do decide to storm the residence, the goal would be to finish everything in three to five minutes maximum, the officer said.
The U.S. ambassador in Lima said Washington has not received any requests for aid from the Peruvians but added that "we are ready to help."
